source.title: Subspace Crystallization in Grokking: Rank Compression Tracks the Phase Transition

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Trains small networks on modular arithmetic and measures delayed test generalization, compression, and interventions relevant to grokking, including held-out seeds and tasks.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own training, test-accuracy, circuit-progress, rank-intervention, and cross-seed results. Cited findings from other studies are not included. Metrics used only to choose a detector or define a threshold are not separately recorded.
record.test_reason: Trains a Nanda-style one-layer transformer and a mean-field MLP on modular arithmetic. It reports delayed generalization (V1), progress measures and cleanup timing (V2), weight-decay, nuclear-norm and rank-cap interventions (V5) and cross-seed equivalence (V6). The main question, whether rank compression causes grokking, is approached with new methods rather than the originals' recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that rank compression is a signature of grokking, not its cause: it follows the onset rather than memorization, and imposing low rank (against a factorized control) or a nuclear-norm penalty does not speed grokking. Judged by outputs, the transformer crystallizes to 8–13 directions per matrix during the transition, alongside cleanup. The MSE MLP does not: its accuracy-based narrowing reflects margin growth, and its late compression tracks AdamW's effective learning rate lr/ϵ.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains mean-field MLPs and one-layer transformers on modular arithmetic and adds time-resolved rank/output measures, rank caps, nuclear-norm penalties, and optimizer comparisons. It does not reproduce either original paper's full experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with architecture and loss (transformer versus MLP; MSE versus cross-entropy), rank cap and matrix selected, weight decay, initialization parameterization, optimizer effective learning rate, and whether direction counts use accuracy or output change.

fits_no_version.finding: For MLP Stage 4, the late effective-rank decrease depends on effective learning rate (lr/ϵ under AdamW); gradient descent or momentum SGD at matched effective learning rate reproduces most or all of it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late post-grokking rank compression in this MLP is governed by effective learning rate and is distinct from the grokking onset.

fits_no_version.finding: Factorizing W1 = AB at full rank speeds MLP grokking 7–8-fold (onset about 1,667–2,000 versus about 12,500 steps) but slows the transformer (14,100 versus 10,500 steps).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameterization alone, without changing capacity, can shorten or lengthen the grokking delay.

record.problems: The tasks are modular arithmetic on cyclic groups, and the paper does not vary training-set size. The two main architectures also differ in loss and training duration. Some intervention arms use five seeds and MLP rank caps use three; several non-grokking transformer controls are small groups. The authors note that Granger tests establish temporal predictive asymmetry, not interventional causation, and base causal conclusions on rank interventions.
record.rows_left_out: Many additional per-checkpoint, per-matrix direction counts and auxiliary geometric metrics are omitted; the included transformer Win direction-count checkpoints and circuit-loss timing capture the central version-2 result. Cross-seed controls in Appendix Table 17 are partly combined where the paper reports them as a single 0.6–1.4% range.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks (the train split is never varied); algorithmic tasks beyond cyclic-group modular arithmetic.
Whether the transformer's cleanup result extends beyond a one-layer transformer on modular addition.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale manipulation.
Not tested: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Critical dataset size and ungrokking below it.
Convergence across architectures or broad hyperparameter settings; transformer cross-seed equivalence.
Not tested. The AdamW-epsilon analysis concerns late rank compression after grokking, not the grokking delay itself; softmax numerical limits are not studied.

missing.what: MLP grokking on held-out tasks ab mod 97 (onset 12,633) and (a+b) mod 113 (onset 15,567), 15/15 seeds each
Cross-entropy MLP groks in only 1/5 seeds at lr 10^-3 but in 5/5 at higher lr; ReLU and GELU MLPs grok 2.6–3.5 times later than quadratic ones
Non-grokked transformers narrow dout only slowly and end 2–9 times wider than grokked seeds (control for the V2 progress measure)
Nuclear-norm penalties λ = 10^-8 and 3×10^-8 leave MLP onset unchanged (12,800 versus 12,700 steps)
MLP seeds use different strongest frequencies (Jaccard 0.05), and their weight subspaces overlap no more than random ones
Transformer uses about 4 key frequencies while the MLP spreads over about 45, i.e. different Fourier solutions across architectures

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T2: the study shares the original modular-arithmetic setting, but its main question (does rank compression cause grokking) is answered with new measures and interventions. V1 links were removed from progress-measure rows. Rank caps below the solution's needed directions were set to cannot_determine. Rows r6 and r7 were re-linked to V5. Rows r29 and r30 were changed from reversed/partial to absent, since onset does not move.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary training-set size to test whether smaller sets require more optimization; it tests modular arithmetic, not algorithmic datasets generally.
The circuit-progress and cleanup analyses are primarily for the one-layer transformer; the study does not establish that the same mechanism holds across architectures or tasks generally.
No non-algorithmic images, text, or molecule tasks are tested.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
The study tests rank caps and a nuclear-norm penalty, but not a critical dataset size or dataset-size-induced ungrokking.
Cross-run equivalence is tested for MLPs on one task; the study does not establish convergence to the same algorithm across architectures or broad hyperparameter settings.
Optimizer swaps test late MLP rank compression, not whether optimizer or numerical artifacts produce or eliminate the grokking delay.

rows.subject: mean-field MLP (15 seeds, aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 128 hidden units; input dimension 194; output dimension 97
rows.operation_detail: Trained on (a+b) mod 97 with a 35% train split for 10^5 steps; measured training and test accuracy.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy during memorization and grokking transition
rows.baseline: Test accuracy stays below 5% during the reported memorization period.
rows.value: Training accuracy 97.8 ± 0.4% by step 8,000; test accuracy 37.0 ± 8.0% at step 10,000 and reaches 95% at tg = 12,633 ± 297; training accuracy reaches 100% during the transition.
rows.uncertainty: Means ± s.d. over 15 seeds, as stated.
rows.note: The paper reports memorization before the test-accuracy rise, followed by high test accuracy.
rows.check: In the MSE MLP the memorization step (9,133 ± 297) precedes onset (12,633 ± 297) by only about 3,500 steps, a short delay. The transformer's delay is far longer.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer (29 grokked seeds, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on (a+b) mod 97 with a 30% train split for 25,000 steps; tracked training fit and test-accuracy onset.
rows.measure: Training fit time and test-accuracy onset
rows.baseline: Training accuracy reaches 99% by the first logged step.
rows.value: All 29 grokked seeds fit the training data within 250 steps; grokking onset ranges from 6,500 to 21,000 steps, with onset defined as first test accuracy ≥ 95%.
rows.note: The paper defines a run as grokked if final test accuracy is at least 95%.
rows.check: Fit time and onset bear on V1 only, not on V2's progress measures.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer (29 grokked seeds, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective-rank change of Win after the initial weight-decay phase and compared its steepest decrease with grokking onset.
rows.measure: Timing of the steepest effective-rank decrease relative to grokking onset
rows.baseline: Timing relative to training-fit step: scatter 4,234 steps around memorization, compared with 506 around onset.
rows.value: Steepest decrease follows onset almost exactly: Pearson r = 0.99, slope 1.02, 95% confidence interval 0.98–1.07; the decrease is 905 ± 506 steps after onset in 27 of 29 seeds.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval and ± values as stated.
rows.note: This row bears on timing and progress during the generalization transition, not on dataset-size dependence.
rows.check: Effective-rank timing is not a V1 measure. As a continuous measure for V2, the drop starts 1,888 ± 992 steps before onset, but its steepest point comes 905 steps after, so it only partly anticipates the jump.

rows.subject: mean-field MLP trained on randomly permuted labels (5 seeds, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on randomly permuted labels as a negative control.
rows.measure: Training accuracy and final test generalization
rows.baseline: Genuine-task MLPs reach 100.0 ± 0.0% test accuracy and 104.0 ± 2.1 final effective rank in the main runs.
rows.value: Random-label networks reach 90% training accuracy at 7,300 ± 274 steps and end at 84 ± 2% training accuracy; they do not grok.
rows.note: This is a negative control, not a test of generalization on the algorithmic task.
rows.check: Random-label MLPs have no generalizable function, so V1 predicts no grokking here. This is a negative control for compression and IPR, not a V1 result.
